title: Inheritance, Templates and Exceptions
subtitle: Inheritance, Templates and Exceptions: build, inspect, test, and apply the concept
description: An interactive, dashboard-focused lesson on inheritance, templates and exceptions, with worked code, deliberate debugging, practical transfer, and five explained application questions.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Inheritance, Templates and Exceptions: foundations and mental model

Inheritance, Templates and Exceptions is not just a syntax topic: it is a way to make the application’s intent explicit. Handle expected failures specifically and keep useful diagnostics. Do not turn failed operations into misleading success or hide defects with arbitrary defaults. In the Code Academy dashboard, that idea matters because A progress tracker can combine standard containers, small functions, and clear data structures. Start by identifying the input, the rule being applied, and the result that a learner should observe. Separate what the code declares from what it actually does at runtime. A name, selector, function, condition, or query should express one clear responsibility. When reading an example, predict its behavior before running or reviewing the output. If the prediction is wrong, trace each meaningful line instead of rewriting everything at once. This habit builds the kind of reasoning that transfers to unfamiliar code, not merely a memory of one sample. The first example introduces the smallest useful version of the idea; later examples test it against variations and edge cases.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Inheritance, Templates and Exceptions: Exceptions transfer control to a handler; user-facing feedback can remain general
blocks.code: try { throw std::runtime_error("save failed"); } catch (const std::exception& error) { std::cerr << "Could not save attempt\n"; }
blocks.output: Exceptions transfer control to a handler; user-facing feedback can remain general.

blocks.text: Example 1 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “try { throw std::runtime_error("save failed"); } catch (const std::exception& error) { std::cerr << "Could not save attempt\n"; }”: Starts a protected operation whose expected failures are handled by a corresponding handler. Expected behavior: Exceptions transfer control to a handler; user-facing feedback can remain general. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A score is converted from external text, and the input may be "eighty". What should occur?
options: Treat the failed conversion as a valid score of zero in every context
Ignore the failure and report success
Display a full private stack trace to the learner
Handle the conversion failure and show a controlled validation message
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Handle the conversion failure and show a controlled validation message. Invalid input should not silently become success; handle expected conversion errors at the boundary.
blocks.reasoning: Invalid input should not silently become success; handle expected conversion errors at the boundary. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Inheritance, Templates and Exceptions: A pure virtual function makes the class an interface-like abstract base
blocks.code: class Reporter { public: virtual std::string report() const = 0; virtual ~Reporter() = default; };
blocks.output: A pure virtual function makes the class an interface-like abstract base.

blocks.text: Example 2 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “class Reporter { public: virtual std::string report() const = 0; virtual ~Reporter() = default; };”: Declares a data type or contract that groups fields and/or behavior. Expected behavior: A pure virtual function makes the class an interface-like abstract base. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A file read fails because the file is missing. Which response is most useful?
options: Catch every error and do nothing
Expose server paths and secrets in the page
Handle the specific I/O failure and keep detailed diagnostics in a protected log
Continue using the missing file’s contents
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Handle the specific I/O failure and keep detailed diagnostics in a protected log. A controlled user message plus safe diagnostics preserves usability without hiding the cause or exposing internals.
blocks.reasoning: A controlled user message plus safe diagnostics preserves usability without hiding the cause or exposing internals. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Inheritance, Templates and Exceptions: implementation, debugging, and edge cases

Implementation quality depends on details that are easy to miss. Handle expected failures specifically and keep useful diagnostics. Do not turn failed operations into misleading success or hide defects with arbitrary defaults. Compare the expected result with the actual result, then ask which smallest change explains any difference. Check the data type, boundaries, execution order, and assumptions about missing or invalid input. For the Code Academy dashboard, A progress tracker can combine standard containers, small functions, and clear data structures. A solution that works only for one perfect input is incomplete. For instance, check empty strings, a zero count, an unavailable resource, an unknown key, or a repeated user action whenever those cases fit the feature. Keep responsibilities small so the cause of a defect can be isolated. The second and third examples show how to make the logic clearer and how to recognize a failure mode. Read the comments and output notes as a guide to reasoning, not as a substitute for inspecting every statement.

blocks.title: Example 3 — Inheritance, Templates and Exceptions: override makes the compiler verify the intended base virtual method
blocks.code: class CourseReporter : public Reporter { public: std::string report() const override { return "Progress ready"; } };
blocks.output: override makes the compiler verify the intended base virtual method.

blocks.text: Example 3 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “class CourseReporter : public Reporter { public: std::string report() const override { return "Progress ready"; } };”: Declares a data type or contract that groups fields and/or behavior. Expected behavior: override makes the compiler verify the intended base virtual method. What if a line changes? If the return path is removed, the caller may receive no usable result even though the calculation ran. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A broad catch block returns a successful result after any exception. What is the core defect?
options: It makes type checking stricter
It turns failures into false success and makes corruption harder to detect
It forces every function to become asynchronous
It guarantees all resources are closed
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: It turns failures into false success and makes corruption harder to detect. Recovery must reflect the actual state; pretending success masks defects and can corrupt progress data.
blocks.reasoning: Recovery must reflect the actual state; pretending success masks defects and can corrupt progress data. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 4 — Inheritance, Templates and Exceptions: Check container state before operations that require an element
blocks.output: Check container state before operations that require an element.

blocks.text: Example 4 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “std::vector<int> scores{4, 5, 3};”: Continues the example’s expression or control block. Read it in order with the preceding declaration and following result. Line 2 — “if (!scores.empty()) std::cout << scores.front();”: Checks a condition or selects a branch; the result determines which path executes. Expected behavior: Check container state before operations that require an element. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: Two database updates must both succeed or both be undone. Which mechanism is designed for that?
options: A transaction with commit on success and rollback on failure
A loop that retries forever
HTML form validation alone
A display-only warning after each update
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: A transaction with commit on success and rollback on failure. Transactions group related operations atomically when used correctly.
blocks.reasoning: Transactions group related operations atomically when used correctly. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Inheritance, Templates and Exceptions: applied challenge and mastery check

Professional practice means verifying the requirement from a learner’s point of view. Handle expected failures specifically and keep useful diagnostics. Do not turn failed operations into misleading success or hide defects with arbitrary defaults. For the Code Academy dashboard, A progress tracker can combine standard containers, small functions, and clear data structures. Finish by following a small test sequence: verify a normal case, a boundary case, and a failure case; confirm the page remains understandable; and check that the result matches the requirement rather than merely appearing plausible. Ask what would happen if one important line were removed, changed, or called in the wrong order. Distinguish a syntax error from a logic error and from an interface or data issue. The final sample brings the concept into a compact applied task, and the questions ask for decisions rather than isolated definitions. A strong answer should be supported by a reason and by a test that could prove or disprove the assumption.

Applied challenge: implement a small Code Academy feature that uses inheritance, templates and exceptions. Define the expected behavior in one sentence, identify the input and output, and choose the simplest code pattern above that fits. Test a normal case and an edge case. Then make one controlled change: remove a condition, alter a value, or change an input shape. Record what breaks and explain why. This is the “do and let me do” part of the lesson: the concept becomes memorable when the learner predicts a result, observes it, and explains the difference.

blocks.question: A failure is expected and the caller can recover. What belongs in the function contract?
options: A silent return value that looks like success
An unconditional retry with no limit
An undocumented global flag
A clear error/result path or a documented exception
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: A clear error/result path or a documented exception. A caller needs a reliable way to distinguish success from a recoverable failure.
blocks.reasoning: A caller needs a reliable way to distinguish success from a recoverable failure. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: Lesson recap: Handle expected failures specifically and keep useful diagnostics. Do not turn failed operations into misleading success or hide defects with arbitrary defaults. Keep the underlying rule in mind when moving to more complex dashboard features. Syntax is the visible surface; reliable reasoning, validation, and testing are the transferable skill.
